content: The studies reviewed were limited to those published in English, Chinese, or Russian and indexed in databases such as Medline, OVID, Chinese Biomedical Literature, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and the Russian e-library. The quality of these studies was evaluated using Drummond’s checklist for economic evaluations. Additionally, a Markov-chain model was developed to assess the cost-effectiveness of novel tuberculosis skin tests (TBSTs) compared to existing tests, such as the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). This model simulated a cohort of individuals transitioning through various stages of tuberculosis (TB) care and incorporated parameters such as TB infection prevalence, treatment initiation and completion rates, progression to active TB, treatment efficacy, and diagnostic test accuracy (sensitivity and specificity). The model parameters, unit costs, and diagnostic accuracy estimates were derived from the literature, including systematic reviews. Manufacturers of TBSTs were contacted to provide cost estimates for the new tests, but only Generium, the producer of Diaskintest, provided detailed cost data, including delivery costs for different volumes. Consequently, the modeling study focused on Diaskintest as a representative of the TBST class. The model was applied to three countries—Brazil, South Africa, and the United Kingdom—and considered three testing strategies: Diaskintest, TST, and IGRAs (Quantiferon-TB Gold In-Tube or Gold Plus). Outcomes included unit costs (in US dollars), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), and incremental net benefits per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. Costs were analyzed from a health system perspective, excluding patient or societal costs. In Brazil and South Africa, Diaskintest was found to be cost-saving compared to TST and IGRAs, with greater health gains (QALYs per patient). In the United Kingdom, Diaskintest resulted in health gains but was more expensive per patient than IGRAs. IGRAs were more costly to implement than TST in Brazil and South Africa but provided health gains. However, in the United Kingdom, IGRAs were cheaper to implement and more cost-effective than TST. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to identify the maximum unit costs at which TBSTs would remain cost-saving or cost-effective. User perspectives on the value, feasibility, usability, and acceptability of diagnostic technologies were also considered. Two systematic reviews synthesized qualitative evidence on end-user values and preferences for TBSTs compared to existing tests (TST and IGRAs). Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted with clinicians, laboratory staff, program officers, and individuals living with TB infection. A discrete choice experiment (DCE) survey was also performed to elicit stated preferences from participants without directly asking for their preferred options. Key end-user values included test accuracy, convenience, positive patient experience, and cost. Participants preferred tests that were easy to administer, accessible in community or primary care settings, and did not require follow-up visits or additional infrastructure. Qualitative evidence suggested that TBSTs are unlikely to create new equity issues and may improve health equity by providing accurate, low-cost tests suitable for resource-limited settings. However, in low-resource settings without existing TST infrastructure, barriers to accessing skin tests would need to be addressed first. Data from the DCE indicated a strong preference for community-based testing over hospital-based testing, which could have implications for health equity. TBSTs were perceived to have greater specificity and sensitivity than TST, which was considered desirable to avoid the consequences of false positives or negatives. However, in countries with existing IGRA infrastructure, TBSTs were not seen as adding value due to comparable accuracy and performance. Broader concerns about skin tests included their dated nature, susceptibility to human error, and interpretation challenges. Implementation considerations included the need for regulatory approval, appropriate communication about the differences between TST and TBSTs, cold chain requirements, skilled staff for administration and interpretation, and effective operational planning for multi-use vials. Single-use vials or smaller-dose vials were preferred to match daily needs. Procurement, stock management, and linkage to care to reduce loss to follow-up were also critical. Global market availability and standardization of TBST reaction measurement and interpretation were emphasized as necessary for successful implementation.
